presentingComplaint: Acutely hot, swollen, exquisitely painful right knee with fever for 36 hours.
history: 63-year-old man with a 10-year history of recurrent podagra (first metatarsophalangeal attacks, 2-3 per year, never fully investigated) presents to the ED with sudden onset of severe right knee pain that woke him from sleep and became unbearable within hours. The joint is grossly swollen, red and too painful to weight-bear. He reports feeling systemically unwell with subjective fevers and rigors, prompting concern from the triage nurse for a joint sepsis emergency. Background of long-standing hypertension (on hydrochlorothiazide, recently up-titrated), obesity, chronic kidney disease stage 3a, and heavy beer intake. No penetrating trauma, no recent intra-articular injection, no prosthetic joint, no skin breach over the knee. Two prior attacks settled with over-the-counter NSAIDs. He has multiple firm, non-tender nodules over the helices of both ears and over the olecranon and first MTP joints.
examination: Distressed, in obvious pain. Right knee is markedly swollen with a tense effusion, overlying erythema, warmth and gross tenderness; passive and active movement severely restricted by pain. No skin ulceration, no fluctuant collection, no lymphangitic streaking, no crepitus. Tophaceous deposits palpable over both auricular helices, right olecranon and both first MTP joints. No other actively inflamed joints. Cardiovascular and respiratory exam unremarkable; no new murmur. No stigmata of endocarditis. Overlying skin intact.

labs.synovial_fluid_crystals: Abundant needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals (intracellular and extracellular) under compensated polarised light

imaging: Plain radiograph right knee: soft-tissue swelling with joint effusion; punched-out juxta-articular erosions with sclerotic overhanging margins and preserved joint space, consistent with chronic tophaceous gout. No chondrocalcinosis. No osteomyelitis or gas. Bedside ultrasound: large anechoic effusion with hyperechoic 'double contour' sign over femoral cartilage and aggregate tophaceous material; no rim-enhancing collection.
microbiology: Synovial fluid Gram stain negative for organisms; aerobic and anaerobic synovial fluid cultures no growth at 48 hours (final at 5 days: no growth). Two sets of blood cultures: no growth. Being non-infective crystal disease, no antimicrobial therapy is indicated.
differentialDiagnoses: Septic (bacterial) arthritis — the key overlapping emergency to exclude given fever, leucocytosis and a single hot joint
Acute monoarticular presentation of rheumatoid or other inflammatory arthritis
finalDiagnosis: Acute crystal (gouty) arthritis of the right knee in a patient with chronic tophaceous gout — clinically mimicking septic arthritis but confirmed by synovial monosodium urate crystals with negative Gram stain and cultures.
citations: ACR Guideline for the Management of Gout 2020
EULAR Recommendations for the Diagnosis of Gout 2018
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e — Gout and Other Crystal-Associated Arthropathies
stewardship: Non-infective inflammatory arthritis: NO antibiotics indicated. The febrile hot single joint mandates urgent arthrocentesis to exclude septic arthritis BEFORE committing to any therapy; empirical antibiotics may be started only while awaiting fluid results if sepsis is genuinely suspected, but here the demonstration of monosodium urate crystals with a negative Gram stain and negative cultures excludes infection and antibiotics must be withheld/stopped. Manage the flare with an anti-inflammatory agent (NSAID, colchicine, or corticosteroid) chosen for CKD stage 3a; defer urate-lowering initiation decisions per ACR guidance and treat comorbid diuretic-driven hyperuricaemia.
contraindications: Avoid/limit NSAIDs given CKD stage 3a (eGFR 52) and hypertension — prefer oral corticosteroid or intra-articular steroid after infection excluded
Reduce colchicine dose in renal impairment and avoid with strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors
Do not start or stop allopurinol acutely during the flare without appropriate anti-inflammatory cover; dose allopurinol to renal function
edgeCases: Crystal arthritis and septic arthritis can coexist — presence of crystals does not fully exclude infection if fluid is frankly purulent or cultures grow, so cultures must still be followed
Thiazide diuretic up-titration is a common precipitant of gout flares and hyperuricaemia
Serum urate may be normal or low during an acute attack; a normal urate does not exclude gout
Chondrocalcinosis on imaging would raise pseudogout (CPPD), which shows rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals
expectedMaiK: Perform urgent arthrocentesis and send synovial fluid for polarised-light crystal analysis, cell count, Gram stain and culture to distinguish crystal arthritis from septic arthritis before committing to therapy; identification of negatively birefringent MSU crystals with negative Gram stain/cultures confirms gout and antibiotics are not indicated.
expectedNextQuestions: Any prosthetic joint, recent joint injection, or skin breach over the knee?
History of previous gout attacks, tophi, or hyperuricaemia?
Recent change in diuretic or other urate-raising drugs, and alcohol intake?
Any immunosuppression or features suggesting bacteraemic seeding of the joint?
expectedInvestigations: Arthrocentesis with synovial fluid polarised-light microscopy for crystals
Synovial fluid white cell count and differential
Synovial fluid Gram stain and aerobic/anaerobic culture
Serum urate, renal function and inflammatory markers (CRP/ESR)
Blood cultures (to help exclude the septic-arthritis differential)

investigations: Arthrocentesis with synovial fluid polarised-light crystal analysis
Synovial fluid cell count, Gram stain and culture

regressionAssertions: Engine must return crystal_arthritis as the leading diagnosis despite fever, leucocytosis and a single hot joint suggestive of septic arthritis.
Arthrocentesis with synovial crystal analysis must be recommended before definitive therapy.
No antibiotics should be recommended once MSU crystals are identified with negative Gram stain and cultures (stewardship tier null).
NSAID caution and preference for corticosteroid/colchicine dosing must reflect CKD stage 3a.
Septic arthritis / cellulitis must appear in the differential but not as the accepted diagnosis.
